children: "The numbers have gone crazy," says Victor DePoalo, a Provincetown restaurateur and real-estate developer. He is referring to his $5 million sale earlier today of a condo that he built for himself in 2019 and has lived in until now. It's the highest price ever paid for a condo in this town at the tip of Cape Cod, according to listing agent Thomas Andrews of Gibson Sotheby's International Realty.

The 2,725-square-foot unit is one of five that DePoalo built on the Bradford Street Extension, which parallels the west end of Commercial Street, the town's main drag. He sold one of the units for $1.8 million when he finished it in 2019. It resold in August for $3.9 million, which was a record condo price in Provincetown until today. The median sales price for condos in Provincetown is just under $1 million, according to Redfin. (The median price for single family homes is more than twice that.)

DePoalo, 64, shared the three-bedroom, five-bathroom condo with his husband and their 12-year-old son. Rare for Provincetown, it has a large, secluded backyard with a saltwater gunite pool. "I'm giving up something I may never be able to get back," he says.
The five condos are decidedly modern, which might have been a problem on Commercial Street but not on Bradford Street Extension, which is outside the city's historic district.

DePoalo, a year-round Provincetown resident whose son attends school there, sold the condo to raise money for a much larger project, a 28,000-square-foot mixed-use building at 185 Commercial Street. DePoalo said he is investing $20 million in the three-story building, which will replace Bubala's By the Bay, a popular restaurant set back from the street behind an extensive outdoor seating area. DePoalo's new building will contain a 100-seat restaurant, nine hotel rooms and 10 condos (two of them designated affordable).

One that won't be designated affordable is the 3,000-square-foot unit being designed for DePoalo and his family. It will have views of Provincetown Harbor and open water beyond. "I've always dreamt of living on the ocean," said DePoalo, who grew up in Schenectady, NY.

The seller of Bubala's is John "Jingles" Yingling, who bought the property in 1994 for $550,000. Yingling also owns Spiritus, the pizza place just up the street that attracts a crowd after the Provincetown bars-mostly gay bars-close. They agreed on a price, Yingling says, of "just under $7 million," with a closing scheduled for October 9.

In Provincetown, where even tiny changes to historic buildings can spark outsize controversies, DePoalo's project has met only scattered opposition. He won the approval of the city's Historic District Commission after making several changes to the building's exterior. John Dowd, who heads the commission, said DePoalo "had no problem tailoring his designs to fit the guidelines of the district."

Now DePoalo is seeking planning board approval. In a letter, Timothy Famulare, the town's Community Development Director, listed several changes to the landscaping and paths around the building that DePoalo will have to make to satisfy the planning board. However, new concerns could be raised at the board's next public meeting, on September 10, Thaddeus J. Soulé, the Town Planner, wrote in an email.

DePoalo is also hoping that a lawsuit brought by 10 Provincetown taxpayers against the town itself will be dismissed. The lawsuit charges Provincetown with approving a 23-foot-wide curb cut where 18 feet is the maximum legal width, raising safety concerns. The curb cut will provide access to a small garage for the new building's condo owners. Abigail Sklar, a lawyer for the town, did not respond to requests for comment.

The son of a general contractor, DePoalo started his career renovating and flipping condos in Boston. He arrived in Provincetown in 2003 and in 2007 he opened Victor's, a thriving restaurant known for its "seafood happy hour." He has also built or renovated several dozen condominiums. He retained one two-bedroom unit where he will live with his family until the new building on Commercial Street is finished.

DePoalo gave the listing for his condo on Bradford Street Extension to Thomas Andrews. The two men met when Andrews, who has a hospitality background, was working at Victor's. "He said he wanted to go into real estate, so I encouraged him," DePoalo says. Andrews joined Gibson Sotheby's soon after he obtained his real estate license in 2024.

Provincetown is in the midst of a building boom that troubles some residents, in part because the developers are often newcomers to the town, with little knowledge of its history and culture. DePoalo, on the other hand, is considered a local. Yingling said he wouldn't have sold to anyone who didn't live in Provincetown and that he was glad that the buyer is DePoalo. DePoalo, in turn, said he hopes to name the condo and hotel portion of the new building for Yingling.

title: A $5 Million Condo Sale Is a Provincetown Record. For Him, It's the Next Step. — WSJ
